note: 1969-70 recession; claims led by 2 months. The GM strike (Sep-Nov 1970) falls inside the event
1973-75 recession (oil embargo); claims on one month after the NBER peak; unemployment leg 7 months later
Scare: claims spike in the severe winter of Jan-Feb 1977 (natural-gas shortages closed plants); unemployment never rose

1980 recession. CHECK: April 1979 is a one-month claims spike (the Teamsters trucking strike and auto layoffs); claims were off May-Sep and back on from Oct 1979. Only 5 quiet months, so the rule joins them; with the October onset the start is 3 months before the NBER peak instead of 9
1981-82 recession; both legs on in the same month; deepest pre-2008 rise
Scare: one week at +25.1% (week ending 1984-11-03), just over the threshold; cause not identified
CHECK: claims-only spell (Oct 1989 and Jan-Feb 1990) 9 months before the 1990 NBER peak; then 7 quiet months before event 8. Early signal of the 1990-91 recession or a scare?
1990-91 recession; both legs on in the same month (3 months after the NBER peak); slow 'jobless' recovery
2001 recession; claims led the unemployment leg by 7 months and the NBER peak by 4 months
Scare by our rule (no NBER recession within 6 months): the late tail of the 2001 'jobless recovery'; unemployment peaked at 6.3% in June 2003
Scare: Hurricanes Katrina and Rita (Aug-Sep 2005); one week over +25%
2007-09 recession; the unemployment leg came first (Feb 2008) and claims followed in Jul 2008
2020 pandemic recession; claims rose about 25-fold in weeks. Excluded from fitting (decision 4)
Scare: claims jump in Jun-Jul 2023 (reported at the time to reflect Minnesota's new summer benefits for school workers and fraudulent claims in Ohio)
Scare: the widely reported Sahm-rule trigger of mid-2024 (July 2024 first printed at 4.3%, now 4.2%; partly faster labor-force growth; 4.4% by Sep 2025); claims never reached +25%
